utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Let the Registrar call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honour. Case number IT-00-39 & 40-PT, the Prosecutor versus Momcilo Krajisnik and Biljana Plavsic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: May I have the appearances.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Judge May. My name is Mark Harmon. Assisting me today is Mr. Alan Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. BRASHICH
utterances.text: Deyan Brashich for the Krajisnik defence. Good afternoon, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAVICH
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honour. Robert Pavich for the Pavich defence, accompanied by Mr. Eugene O'Sullivan and Mr. Peter Murphy.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: The purpose of this hearing is a Status Conference in this case to monitor progress. Mr. Harmon, if we could deal with the outstanding issues, or Mr. Tieger. I don't know who is going to deal with it. Really, the matters around which this hearing revolve are ensuring that we are as far as possible on track to at least have the Prosecution case ready and the matters which have to be disclosed, that the documents which are still subject to translation are at least identified as far as possible so that the Trial Chamber can give what assistance it can in that respect, and then to fix a timetable for the start of the case, if possible. Let me begin by saying this: that there is an issue at the moment. It's not for resolution, but can I make it plain to the Prosecution that in the final brief due on the -- now on the 31st of October, the Trial Chamber will expect that the Prosecution case is put in full in respect of the linkage of the accused to the various counts in the indictment. A mere general statement of the Prosecution case, for instance, the background and the law, while relevant, is not the core issue now. The core issue is to explain how it is that the Prosecution say that each of these accused is guilty on each count. The Defence should understand that so that they can prepare their case, and of course the Court should understand it in order that it can conduct the case. The theory of responsibility, I think it is referred to, in some quarters, and that should be plain. Now, turning from there to matters of translation and disclosure. Can we begin by the exhibits? As I understand the position at the moment, there are just over 2.000 exhibits which have been identified. As I also understand it, most of those have been translated but not all. It would be helpful to know roughly how many are untranslated in order that we can perhaps approach the Registry to try and see if more resources can't be made available in order to have translation completed.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Your Honour, in trying to collect this data for this Status Conference, I have been informed that the number of exhibits that have been disclosed to date are 2.574, 209 of which remain untranslated.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Let me just get that, 2.574 disclosed. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: And that is only of the exhibits that have been disclosed thus far. There have been another large number of exhibits that have been identified and are in the queue for translation, and when we receive those exhibits back from the Language Service Section, it's our intention to disclose them upon receipt, and in that respect, we have been engaged in that process as was promised at one of the earlier Status Conferences, that is, when we receive from the Language Service Section, we will disclose immediately. And we have made disclosures to the Defence on December the 5th, 7th, 12th, 24th, and 26th, and it is our intention to continue to making disclosures upon receipt of translated documents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Now, what sort of figure are we looking at here of documents which are untranslated?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: The number -- the figure I was given, the number of documents that have been identified at this point as additional documents are 2.801, and of that lot, 504 have been translated.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: These are all documents on which you intend to rely; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: So we are looking at a figure of 2.500 or so untranslated documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: By the current data available to me, that's correct. Now, I can tell Your Honour - Mr. Tieger can expand on this - we have taken efforts in-house to try to alleviate the problem that is obviously inherent in not having translations. Some of these documents we are prepared -- we have requested from the Language Service Section that they give us only draft translations at this point in time, given the fact that the Language Service Section drafts are quite accurate. That will permit us to get more documents in the English language to the Defence, and we will follow up with final translations after the 31st of October. So that's one way we anticipate being able to increase the number of translated documents that we can pass to the Defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: An issue arose about the core documents. Now, when you disclose, on the 31st of October, your final list, which I anticipate will be disclosed then, those core documents should be identified. I think you've identified 400 and there are another 400 to be identified.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Yes. In respect of the actual number, we have had a discussion previously. The number 800 is a number I inherited when I came on the case at the conclusion of the Krstic case and the number of core documents will be decided, obviously by me and by members of my trial team, but we will be able identify what we consider to be core documents in our 31 October final pre-trial brief.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: The next issue is videos. The original figure we had were 20 videos, none transcribed, as I understand it, or translated. Now, Mr. Harmon, can you tell me the latest position in regard to these video recordings?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Yes, I was informed by Ms. Featherstone that I would be getting this inquiry at 2.00 this afternoon, and unfortunately the person who is involved with running the video aspect of this pre-trial preparation is in New York and unavailable to me. I can't give you any numbers, but I'm prepared to give Your Honours a written submission with regard to any question you may have about videos, upon his return, which will be next week. What I can tell you is that, first of all, in terms of getting translations of those videos from the Language Service Section, it's a very onerous task. First of all, we have -- we, the Office of the Prosecutor, have to go through those and prepare draft transcripts of those. Then we have to take those transcripts and submit those transcripts to the Language Service Section with the video. So it's a two-step process. The end product, of course, is a final transcript from that particular video selection. We are prepared to make available to the Defence, if we haven't already done so, a master reel with all of the video clips that we have identified thus far. The benefit of that is, one, it will assist them right now to view these video clips. The clips are in a language the accused understand, and we will try to get the translations of the videos upon which we intend to rely as soon as we can. We have -- I've asked my assistant -- and he's not here so I don't know if this has been provided to the Defence, but we have also prepared an index with an identification of the video, as I recall, the date of the video and a very short summary of what it is, to accompany any video reel that we provide to the Defence. So we are trying to give them as much information as we can, that we have at our disposal, now, but the actual, finalised transcripts in trial form will not be ready by the 31st of October and obviously will take a position in a line in the queue with every other document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Given the cumbersome nature of the process, it may be sensible to review the videos and to see how much use they really are. Videos are very interesting in cases, one finds, but they don't really add a great deal to things. So it may be helpful to do that, and perhaps you can let us have a written submission on it in two weeks.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: That would be fine. Just so you know, we have already done the first review process. In other words, we have gone through the video archives that we have and we have selected from those archival materials that we have a preliminary selection. It is that selection that we are providing. We have already provided to the Defence, or we will be providing to the Defence, in other words, our selection. So, yes, I can give Your Honour a written submission on the status of the videos in two weeks.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Thank you. Next, turning to the -- to matters arising from witnesses, and in that connection, there seem to be three or four issues. The first, again, is the translation issue. Now, the figures which I have are a total of 337 potential witnesses, of whom something in the region of 240 have been translated, but in fact, when it comes to the number of witness statements, I understand the vast majority have been translated. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: I've been handed the latest statistics by my assistant who is in charge of developing these statistics, and there are approximately 1.200 witness statements, including previous testimony before the Tribunal. Approximately 860 of those have been translated. I'm informed that the 860 translations are witness statements. It does Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. not include previous testimony before the ICTY. And in that regard, we're prepared to give audio cassettes of the previous testimony. If it's a Bosnian-language speaker, I will provide that to the Defence in B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Well, that seems a sensible start. I'm just going to make an inquiry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Harmon, what we will do is this: that we will take this translation problem up with the Registry and see if some priority cannot be given, as this case must come on, and at the moment, this is holding it up. I am reminded that in some cases, in the case of the videos, to go back to that, the Senior Legal Officer has identified some which have translations because we've had them in other cases, and perhaps we can -- when you're looking at that, you can review it. As for the other translations, we must see what other resources can be made available to try and expedite matters, and we'll have in mind the suggestion of audio cassettes, and in fact, perhaps you can make those available on a voluntary basis, and it may expedite matters to some extent.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: We're prepared to do that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Thank you. The next issue about witnesses is the question of redactions. Now, I know that some applications have been made. At the moment, until there are orders, of course, unredacted statements should be disclosed. So it's a question of making the applications for the redactions that you want.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: We have made -- we filed applications in every case that we have identified a witness who testified previously under a pseudonym, and we're awaiting the decisions in those particular cases. Once we get those decisions we will turn over to the Defence unredacted statements.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Thank you. Next, the Rule 92 bis statements. Now, I understand the position there to be that 156 witnesses have been identified as potentially candidates for such testimony. I think the best we can do in that regard is that it's not possible, as I understand as has been suggested, for the Trial Chamber to give any sort of indication. The Rule clearly reads that it's the party that's got to produce the statements and then the Trial Chamber rules. That means that the work has got to be done, and I think the best that one could do to expedite it will be for a date for conclusion so that the Trial Chamber, which is going to conduct this case, will be in a position to decide. And it's a matter to which we can return, but I would anticipate next year, early next year would be the date for a final conclusion, which would give you three or four months to get it done.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: I can give Your Honour some current information. The majority -- the majority of these 92 bis witness declarations, we have prepared missions to collect and on the condition that we receive, and I expect to receive, the full cooperation of the Registrar in identifying and nominating Presiding Officers to assist us. We could collect the majority of these 92 bis declarations by the 21st of December of this year. Now, obviously that -- when I say "the majority," there will be some people who fall through the cracks, who we simply are unable to locate or will have difficulties meeting with us, and there may be a small percentage that go beyond the 21st. Now, those are -- the majority of witnesses are located in Bosnia, and we've already prepared the missions, we've organised the missions, it's been staffed, and we expect, as I say, to complete the majority of witnesses whom were found in Bosnia by that date. That leaves a smaller number of witnesses for whom we're seeking 92 bis declarations, but they're scattered over 11 different countries, and in that regard, we will endeavour to also complete those by the 21st of December. But as I say, that depends upon everything working in sync. We have had some discussions with the Registrar's office about the nomination of Presiding Officers, and all of what I have said in the time schedule that I'm now presenting to Your Honour depends upon the nomination of these Presiding Officers to accompany the missions that are now -- have been identified and will embark. We intend to start these missions, I might add, on the 8th of October, preliminarily to go into the field, and we intend to start taking these 92 bis declarations on the 15th of October. So we have a full programme, a full agenda, an ambitious agenda that we hope to complete successfully by the 21st of December.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well. The final matter, I think, on this topic is the question of experts. As far as experts are concerned - again, I'll be told if I am correct about this - I understand that 2 of the 11 intended expert witnesses' statements or reports have been disclosed. The remainder are in various stages of preparation. Is that the latest position?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: That is correct. We filed two 94 bis declarations regarding the exhumations at Brcko on the 1st of June, 2001 and the Defence replied by saying they wished to reserve their right to cross-examine the experts who have been identified in those submissions. On the 25th of July, 2001, we filed the expert statements of three additional expert witnesses. Those three additional statements related to 14 exhumations that were conducted by the Bosnian authorities and are relevant to our indictment. Now, those reports were in B/C/S when we filed those expert statements. In other words, they were in a language the accused understood. But on the 30th of July, those filings were rejected. I'm not sure whether it was by the Trial Chamber or whether it was by the Registrar, but we were not permitted to complete those filings, and we were advised that what those filings lacked were an English translation of the statement of the expert and colour photographs as opposed to the black and white copies that we submitted with our report. When we received that information on the 30th of July, we immediately submitted for English language translation the expert reports and we made a request to the Bosnian authorities for colour copies of the black and white photographs that we had submitted. I can report to Your Honour now that we have received the translations for 5 of those 14 reports, but we have not yet received the colour photographs. We are prepared to file the five reports, translated into English and B/C/S, now, to be followed by the colour photographs when we receive the colour photographs. And as to the remaining nine reports that we still await translations, we can only file those when we receive the translations. So --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: These are all exhumation reports?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I don't know what issue could arise about them, but I'll investigate that with the Defence. We will also investigate this question of the filing. I can't understand why it's necessary to have coloured photographs as opposed to black and white.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Well, we agree with you on that, Judge May. As to the other expert reports, I can report that those are in an ongoing process of being prepared, and obviously, as Mr. Tieger said at the last conference, we will file those upon receipt, unless there is a sensitivity, a particular sensitivity, that is relating to the particular report, in which case we will abide by the terms of the rule and file them 21 days before the expert is -- will be testifying.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: At the last provisional release hearing, Mr. Tieger told the Trial Chamber that you were making every effort to be ready in February. Do I understand that to be the position?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: We are continuing in that effort, and Mr. Tieger was absolutely right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: So as far as readiness is concerned, may I take it that as far as you can see at the moment, you would be ready for trial in February?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: I would say, obviously, with the problems that we have in translations, it's contingent upon getting all of the documents that we need prepared, and all of the declarations that we anticipate for purposes of 92 bis available, and all of the expert reports that are currently in the process of being finalised. If all of those -- if we hit on all of those cylinders, then, yes, but given the problems that -- the bottleneck caused by language service difficulties, that are quite obvious to us, and felt by us, and the competing needs of other major cases, that's the one -- those are the reservations that I have. But we are endeavouring to meet any order of this Court in good faith.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: May I add one additional piece of information for Your Honour? We have reviewed and continue to review our witness list, and, for the record, we will withdraw at least one witness from our witness list and I will state, that is a witness who has been identified as KRAJ 242 who was found on page 166 of our provisional pre-trial brief submission. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I turn to the Defence. Perhaps we could deal, first of all, with the issue which has been raised about expert reports, and then come on to talk about timing. As far as the exhumation reports are concerned, are there issues which rise about -- arise about these exhumations which you may want to cross-examine about?

utterances.speaker: MR. BRASHICH
utterances.text: Your Honour, the Krajisnik Defence has filed a reservation of rights. I have not, as of today, spoken to a forensic expert to decide whether or not cross-examination would be necessary, and Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. that is the reason why I reserved the Krajisnik's Defence's right to do so, but anticipate that before the end of the year, I would be given guidance by such an expert to do so. I had raised the issue of hiring an expert with the office of the legal aid, OLAD, and I have not had an answer as yet as to the ability to retain the services of such an expert.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Pavich, are you in a similar position?

utterances.speaker: MR. PAVICH
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. I think that once we have received the final brief, pre-trial brief, of the Prosecutor, we will be in a position to make a final decision. We are simply reserving our right at this point, and it's quite possible there will be no issue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Very well. Well, if that matter could be addressed by the Defence as soon as possible. We don't want witnesses brought here unnecessarily when, in fact, there's going to be no dispute about what they say. I'll hear any points which the Defence want to raise, but the Trial Chamber want to raise various matters. The first, really, consists of the question of a timetable. This case should be brought on for trial. This has been said numerous times, but it must still be in mind. The position at the moment is that the finalised Prosecution pre-trial brief is due on 31st of October. Under the original timetable, which allowed -- which was for the 31st of August, the Defence pre-trial briefs were due on the 30th of November. That was one month after the finalised brief. Now, are the Defence going to ask for more time to produce pre-trial briefs or are they content with the date of the 30th of November? Are they going to ask for more time? It would be useful to know, and if so, when, so that we can try and timetable the rest of this case. Mr. Brashich.

utterances.speaker: MR. BRASHICH
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. I'm mindful of Your Honour's comments with regard to the final pre-trial brief. The Krajisnik defence filed with the Plavsic defence a joint-position statement as to the state of the final pre-trial brief as it now exists. It would be upon receipt of the final pre-trial brief that would give us an indication of a timetable. The other matter which would affect the filing of the Defence pre-trial brief would be the completion of the translations. During the Chamber's questioning of the Prosecution, the way that I did my arithmetic, is that we have 2.574 translated, more or less, exhibits. We have outstanding 2.500, roughly. Now, if it has taken from the date of my client's arrest, which was April of 2000, to today to translate 2.574 documents, then I take it it's going to take roughly the same amount of time, a year and a half, to get the balance of the 2.500.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I suspect that's not been the problem. I expect the problem has been identification earlier on.

utterances.speaker: MR. BRASHICH
utterances.text: ... Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Anyway, that sort of timetable, obviously, isn't acceptable --

utterances.speaker: MR. BRASHICH
utterances.text: I understand, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: -- and it must be -- it must be hurried up.

utterances.speaker: MR. BRASHICH
utterances.text: Based on the hurrying up that Your Honour refers to, that would have a bearing on the time that we would be ready to be able to file the Defence pre-trial brief.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: At the moment, what I have in mind is that you should have the three months, which was the time originally allowed, which would take you until the 31st of January. Now, I recognise that there may still be difficulties about translation, but subject, of course, to those being overcome, I would -- I would have that date in mind.

utterances.speaker: MR. BRASHICH
utterances.text: Could I have --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: One at a time.

utterances.speaker: MR. BRASHICH
utterances.text: Could I have a moment to speak to Mr. Pavich so that we do not end up in disagreement in open court?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. BRASHICH
utterances.text: We have agreed to agree, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: What are you agreed to agree on?

utterances.speaker: MR. PAVICH
utterances.text: We have agreed that Mr. Brashich will allow me to address the Court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAVICH
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think that much will depend upon the product that the Prosecutor is able to create by 31 October. The more useful the final pre-trial brief, the more expeditiously we'll be able to respond to it. From our point of view, we would much rather have a pre-trial brief that is helpful to us and to the Court, that is produced regardless of whether it's 30 October or 30 November, rather than getting a pre-trial brief that may be of little help to us and to the Court because of the time constraints and because of the problems that the Prosecutor has already identified. So from that point of view, we would be, I think, in a much better position if the Prosecutor is able to give us a pre-trial brief on 30 October or perhaps somewhat later than that if the final product can be more helpful. I think it would be ultimately much more expeditious for us to perhaps give the Prosecutor, if the Prosecutor feels it would be helpful, a bit more time than we would be in a position, I think, to respond much more quickly and in the long-run, I think we'll all get to the end point a bit more quickly. And I would like Mister -- if the Court please, Mr. O'Sullivan to raise a couple of the logistical and technical points that I think support what I'm saying.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'll address these points because I'm a little more familiar with the disclosure than Mr. Pavich. In listening to what's been said today, of course we've identified numbers of documents, 2.500 documents, but of course the important thing, it seems, is the number of pages those documents represent, and that is, of course, also true for the 460 statements, the number of pages which will impact on the date at which translation is completed, which will impact on, I would say, the Prosecution's ability to file this meaningful pre-trial brief, which has the ripple effect of impacting on the date for our Defence pre-trial brief, not to put aside the videos that must be transcribed and translated. Since we're in a Status Conference, and if I can make a request through Your Honour to the Prosecution, there is some confusion in the disclosure that we've had so far because of the fact we've had the so-called core documents, the 392 core documents which were disclosed in July that have an index. We now have an index of some 2.500 documents now, and if it's at all possible to get one master index from the Prosecution, that would greatly assist us. If I can give you one example. We looked through the August 31st disclosure. We come to a document that says "Already provided." Well, we have to search around quite a bit where that is, and it's just not a very convenient or efficient way to work. And I know that in the last 65 ter conference held by Mrs. Featherstone, I believe there was an attempt there to -- for us to find out, based on the minutes that I've read, to what extent the core documents from July are also contained in the August 31st disclosure. And things like that would assist us greatly in working through these documents at this point, so when we get the final product we'll be up to speed and land with our wheels spinning, as it were. One final --

utterances.speaker: MR. BRASHICH
utterances.text: Could I interrupt you, Mr. O'Sullivan? And I take the blame for this, Your Honour. We were talking about the already-provided, omitted. I attended a Rule 65 ter conference solo, without the Plavsic defence. I spoke to Mr. Tieger, and he explained to me that these documents were not omitted but this was an internal method of keeping their documents sequential and that he would provide us with a list which would not have the documents omitted. They were, in fact, all disclosed. Mea culpa, I did not give this information to the Plavsic Defence. I should have and I apologise. As I said, I apologised to the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well. Yes, Mr. O'Sullivan?

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: The final matter that we discussed at the last Status Conference was the issue of reciprocal discovery which we have triggered and which we are in the process of working with the Prosecution on, and today we have sent a request to the Prosecution, which we think is the first step of the ongoing process of providing specificity of what it is we are seeking, which we submit is material to the preparation of our case. As Your Honour knows, we have put our motion in abeyance in an attempt to work with the Prosecution on this matter, and as I said, we have a letter into the Prosecution, and I think we can hopefully continue to work with the Prosecution on this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Well, any cooperation is to be encouraged. Having heard what's been said, I think it right to fix this timetable: To put the pre-trial briefs for the Defence back to the 31st of January; to fix a Pre-Trial Conference now for the 21st of February, which is a Thursday, with a view to starting a trial in the week of the 8th of April. That week is selected because it is, in fact, the week after Easter. It is six months from now. And every effort should be made to start the trial then. There may be difficulties, if it's not started Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. then, of getting a Trial Chamber to hear it. Now, one understands the difficulties which all parties are facing, but it's important that there is a timetable so that everyone is working towards a time for the start of the trial. There may come a time when the amount of Prosecution material has simply to be cut down, and if that is not done by the Prosecution, it will have to be done by the Trial Chamber, and if matters are not ready on time, eventually the Trial Chamber will have to determine to exclude them. That time has not come yet, but it may come in due course. Likewise, although the Trial Chamber recognises the difficulties which the Defence have in the present state of disclosure, nonetheless, every effort must be made to press this case forward. Now, having announced those dates, I of course will hear any submissions that are made. I fully understand that if material isn't ready, there may be difficulty keeping to them, but it is intended that those should be the dates. I would add this: That it would be sensible to have one further Status Conference while this Trial Chamber is in its present composition, which would be the 7th of November, which would be the next Status Conference. It would be sensible for the new Trial Chamber to have a Status Conference either before the recess in December or early January. I don't know if anyone has any submissions about that or indeed about any of the other dates which have been suggested. Mr. Harmon, as far as the Prosecution is concerned?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: No, I have nothing, Your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Does it make any difference to you whether it's the middle of December or the beginning of January? I'm sorry, the recess, as I remember, starts about the 15th of December. I will be reminded. There is a Plenary. It starts on the 17th, but there is a Plenary for three days. I think the last available date will be the 12th of December. Alternatively, the 9th of January, the week of the 8th, 9th of January.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: We are -- Judge May, we are at your disposal, we are here, we are available to meet any conference or Pre-Trial Conference or Status Conference that the Court thinks is appropriate.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. BRASHICH
utterances.text: With regard to the Krajisnik Defence, in light of Christmas on January 7th, I would urge the first week of December, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAVICH
utterances.text: The Plavsic Defence has the same schedule. Christmas is 7 January so it would be either 9 or 10 January, or in December, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Well, the most convenient might be December. The week starts, the relevant week, starts on the 10th of December. Tuesday, the 11th of December. There is a matter I want to raise with the Senior Legal Officer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I've raised with the Senior Legal Officer whether it would be sensible to fix a date now for the next meeting. Rather than do that, what I shall invite the parties to do is to remain here and discuss with her the -- a suitable date for the next Rule 65 ter meeting. Now, unless there are any other matters, the Court will adjourn. Anybody? Anybody want to raise anything? Court will rise.

procedural_notes.text: [The Court and Senior Legal Officer confer]
--- Whereupon the Status Conference adjourned at
